  sensitive or forbidden writes. It does not silently drop them.

### Bound adapter scope

A tenant policy crosses the runtime/adapter boundary as an opaque
`BoundAdapterScope`. Create it with `bindAdapterScope(apply)`. Adapters must
apply it to list, get, update and delete operations and fail closed when a
resource requires scope but no binding is present.

`resolveScopeApplier(ctx)` is that fail-closed rule, shared by the first-party
adapters: it returns the bound predicate, `null` when the resource declares
none, and throws `FlowpanelAccessError` when one is required but missing. An
adapter that resolves scope by hand must refuse the query in the same case.

### Series helpers

`previousRange` and `fillDays` are pure date helpers for dashboard queries, and
are documented with the widgets that consume them — see
[Series helpers](/docs/reference/widgets#series-helpers).

### Post-commit effects

Post-commit audit, realtime or revalidation failures do not turn a committed
mutation into a false failure. They appear as a `FlowpanelWarning` in result
metadata; `FlowpanelWarningCode` is `audit_failed`, `realtime_failed`, or
`revalidation_failed`.

### Result envelope

Every protected controller and v1 JSON CRUD endpoint returns
`FlowpanelResult<T>`:

```ts excerpt
type FlowpanelResult<T> =
  | { ok: true; data: T; meta: FlowpanelResultMeta }
  | { ok: false; error: FlowpanelResultError };
```

`FlowpanelResultMeta` carries the request id and optional warnings.
`FlowpanelResultError` carries a stable `FlowpanelErrorCode`, a safe message,
optional field errors and request id. `FLOWPANEL_ERROR_STATUS` is the canonical
code-to-HTTP-status table.

- `errorResult(error, requestId)` converts known errors to the envelope and
  redacts unexpected failures to `internal`.
- `resultResponse(result)` produces a JSON `Response` with the canonical status.
- `reportUnexpectedError(error, context, onError)` invokes `hooks.onError` at
  most once for the same error object. `ErrorContext` includes request,
  operation, actor, IP and user-agent diagnostics but no submitted secrets.

These helpers are public for runtime authors. Ordinary actions should throw a
documented FlowPanel error or return an `ActionResult`, then let the built-in
runtime normalize it.

Generated-UI form, drawer, action, import, restore and SSE routes predate the
v1 client protocol and keep their compact, route-specific response shapes for
compatibility. Use `createFlowpanelClient` or protected controllers when a
custom surface needs the structured envelope above.

## Adapter contract

What FlowPanel needs from a database layer, method by method.

Docs: https://flowpanel.tech/docs/reference/adapters

Documented types: Adapter, ResourceIntrospection, ColumnMeta, drizzleAdapter, prismaAdapter, bullmqAdapter, DrizzleAdapterOptions, PrismaAdapterOptions, BullMQAdapterOptions, toCsv, toJson

The adapter is the only part of FlowPanel that talks to your database.
Implement this interface to support an ORM that has no shipped adapter — nothing
else in the framework issues a query.

Shipped adapters: [`drizzleAdapter`](/docs/introduction/drizzle) and
[`prismaAdapter`](/docs/introduction/prisma).

### Adapter

`Adapter`

| Property | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `kind` | `AdapterKind` | Which ORM this adapter wraps. Shipped adapters use `"drizzle"` / `"prisma"`. |
| `db` | `DB` | The client handed to every `ctx.db`. |
| `transaction?` | `(run: (db: DB) => Promise<T>) => Promise<T>` | Execute work against one transaction-bound database handle. |
| `introspect` | `(ref: Ref) => ResourceIntrospection` | Describe a table: its columns, types and primary key. |
| `inferSchema` | `(ref: Ref) => { create: z.ZodTypeAny; update: z.ZodTypeAny; select: z.ZodTypeAny; }` | Derive validation schemas from the table, used when a resource sets no `schema`. |
| `list` | `(ref: Ref, ctx: ListQueryContext<unknown>) => Promise<ListResult<unknown>>` | One page of rows, honoring filters, sort, search, scope and soft delete. |
| `get` | `(ref: Ref, ctx: ItemQueryContext) => Promise<unknown \| null>` | A single row by id, or null. Must respect tenant scope. |
| `create` | `(ref: Ref, ctx: MutationContext<unknown>) => Promise<unknown>` | Insert a row. Must reject rows that fall outside the caller's scope. |
| `update` | `(ref: Ref, ctx: MutationContext<unknown>) => Promise<unknown \| null>` | Update a row by id, or return null when it does not exist in scope. |
| `delete` | `(ref: Ref, ctx: MutationContext<unknown>) => Promise<void>` | Delete a row — or stamp `ctx.softDelete.column` when soft delete is on. |
| `restore?` | `(ref: Ref, ctx: MutationContext<unknown>) => Promise<void>` | Clear the soft-delete stamp. Without it, the admin hides the restore button. |
| `sql?` | `(strings: TemplateStringsArray, ...values: unknown[]) => Promise<Row[]>` | Run one read-only statement and return its rows, as a tagged template. Every value arrives as a bound parameter; an implementation must never interpolate one into the SQL text. Without it, `ctx.sql` throws. |
| `count?` | `(ref: Ref, where?: Record<string, unknown>) => Promise<number>` | Count matching rows without reading them. `where` is the same filter shape `list` receives. Without it, FlowPanel counts through `list` with an empty projection, which is one more query but never wrong. |
| `applyMigration?` | `(id: string, sql: string) => Promise<void>` | Optional migration support, used by `flowpanel migrate`. The CLI's earlier `listAppliedMigrations` result may be stale. Implementations that support concurrent migrators must serialize and recheck `id` at the database boundary. |
| `runMigrationSql?` | `(sql: string) => Promise<void>` |  |
| `listAppliedMigrations?` | `() => Promise<Set<string>>` |  |
| `markMigrationApplied?` | `(id: string) => Promise<void>` |  |

`Ref` is whatever you accept in `resource(ref, …)` — a Drizzle table object, a
Prisma delegate, or your own descriptor. `DB` is the client you expose as
`ctx.db` everywhere.

`kind` is `AdapterKind` — `"drizzle" | "prisma" | (string & {})`. The shipped
kinds autocomplete; a third-party adapter picks its own label. Nothing in
FlowPanel branches on it.

`kind`, `db`, `introspect`, `inferSchema`, `list`, `get`, `create`, `update`
and `delete` are required. `restore` is optional — an adapter without it makes
the admin hide the restore button rather than fail at runtime. `sql` and `count`
are optional too, and back [`ctx.sql` and `ctx.count`](/docs/reference/contexts#raw-sql-and-counts)
in a widget query. `applyMigration`
and `listAppliedMigrations` are optional too and power `flowpanel migrate`;
without both, that command exits before executing SQL. The older
`runMigrationSql` and `markMigrationApplied` hooks remain typed for adapter
compatibility. The CLI can compose both as a temporary upgrade path and prints
a warning because that legacy pair cannot keep SQL and its bookkeeping record
atomic. Implement `applyMigration(id, sql)` before relying on rollback safety.

Both shipped adapters execute a migration and write its applied ID through one
adapter operation. The CLI's earlier applied-ID list is only a snapshot, so an
adapter that permits concurrent migrators must serialize and recheck the ID at
the database boundary. A duplicate ID becomes a no-op only after that recheck.

PostgreSQL and SQLite keep every statement and the marker in one transaction —
Drizzle and Prisma both take a lock inside it (a PostgreSQL advisory lock, a
SQLite write lock) and recheck the ID before executing anything.

MySQL implicitly commits DDL, so no tool can promise rollback for an arbitrary
MySQL file: review migrations, make DDL restart-safe, back up production data,
and apply them in a controlled release step. Drizzle pins one connection and
holds a `GET_LOCK` advisory lock. Prisma cannot pin a connection, so it claims
a durable row in `_flowpanel_migration_claims` instead: the claim serializes
migrators, survives a crashed one, and records the statement a failed run
stopped at. A failed claim stops later runs until you repair the schema and
delete that row, so a half-applied file is never silently retried.

Because the lock protocol and the SQL dialect differ per provider,
`prismaAdapter` takes a required `provider` — the same value as the
`datasource` block in `schema.prisma`.

Both adapters split ordinary multi-statement SQL safely. They reject
dialect-specific procedural scripts (for example SQLite/MySQL trigger bodies or
stored procedures) before execution unless the body uses PostgreSQL dollar
quoting, and Prisma also rejects MySQL executable comments and client
directives such as `DELIMITER`, `SOURCE` and `.read`. Apply those files through
the ORM's native migration workflow or a dialect-native runner; a rejected file
is never recorded as applied.

### Raw SQL

`sql` is a tagged template, not a string API: it receives the literal parts and
the interpolated values separately, and every value must reach the database as a
bound parameter. An implementation that assembles a string is wrong — that is
the injection this capability exists to avoid.

`count(ref, where)` takes the same filter shape `list` reads from `ctx.filters`,
including `"__null__"` and `"__notnull__"`. It carries no scope binding, so
FlowPanel only calls it when the resource has no tenant predicate to apply; a
scoped resource is counted through `list` with an empty projection instead. Every
other guard — `requireRole`, `access`, `fieldAccess` and the soft-delete term — is
applied before the call, so which path runs never changes the answer. Implement
`count` anyway: it saves a query on every unscoped count.

Both capabilities run on the adapter's own `db`, never a per-request handle: they
are outside any open `adapter.transaction` and outside session settings a host
applies per request, such as the `SET` a row-level-security scheme relies on.

Two helpers keep a third-party adapter's behaviour identical to the shipped ones:

```ts excerpt
import { parseSqlRows, sanitizeSqlParams } from "@flowpanel/kit";

async function sql<Row>(strings: TemplateStringsArray, ...values: unknown[]) {
  const rows = await driver.query(strings, sanitizeSqlParams(values));
  return parseSqlRows<Row>(rows);
}
```

`sanitizeSqlParams` turns a `Date` into an ISO-8601 string and a `bigint` into
decimal text, and does the same to an array's own values. `parseSqlRows` reads
every string shaped exactly like a zoneless `YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss` as a UTC `Date`,
because a free-form statement has no column types to consult; pass
`{ parseDates: false }` to hand every value through as the driver returned it,
which is what both shipped adapters' `parseDates` option does.

An array is one value to a driver, and the two shipped adapters disagree about it.
Drizzle expands `${ids}` into a placeholder list, so `where id in (${ids})` works.
Prisma binds the array as a single parameter, so the same template fails and the
Postgres form is `where id = any(${ids})` — or build the list with `Prisma.join`.
Portable configs pass one value per placeholder.

Both shipped adapters normalise the driver's own row shape first: node-postgres
answers `{ rows }`, postgres-js and the SQLite drivers the array itself, and
mysql2 `[rows, fields]`.

### ResourceIntrospection

Returned by `introspect`. This is what lets a resource declare `columns: ["id",
"email"]` and get working controls, filters and validation for free.

`ResourceIntrospection`

| Property | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `string` | Table name, used as the resource's default `name`. |
| `columns` | `ColumnMeta[]` |  |
| `primaryKey` | `string` |  |

### ColumnMeta

`ColumnMeta`

| Property | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `string` |  |
| `type` | `"string" \| "number" \| "boolean" \| "date" \| "json" \| "enum" \| "array" \| "reference"` | Normalized type. Decides the default form control and filter. |
| `nullable` | `boolean` |  |
| `unique` | `boolean` |  |
| `primaryKey` | `boolean` |  |
| `enumValues?` | `readonly string[]` | Allowed values, for `enum` columns. |
| `references?` | `{ table: string; column: string }` | Foreign key target, when the column references another table. |
| `maxLength?` | `number` |  |
| `readable?` | `boolean` | Whether this column may be selected and returned by the adapter. |
| `writableOnCreate?` | `boolean` | Whether create input may contain this column. |
| `writableOnUpdate?` | `boolean` | Whether update input may contain this column. |
| `generated?` | `boolean` | Database-computed column that must not be accepted as input. |
| `hasDefault?` | `boolean` | The database or ORM fills the column when the insert omits it. |
| `sensitive?` | `boolean` | Adapter-discovered secret. Always excluded from generated read projections. |

`type` is consulted in exactly one place: the fully generated form a resource
gets when it declares neither `create.fields` nor `update.fields`. The mapping
is short, and everything not listed falls through to a text input:

| `ColumnMeta.type` | Generated form control |
| --- | --- |
| `number` | `number` |
| `boolean` | `checkbox` |
| `date` | `datetime-local` |
| `json` | `json` |
| `string`, `enum`, `array`, `reference` | `text` |

Two things this table does **not** promise:

- **There is no filter inference.** A bare string in `filters` always resolves
  to a `text` filter regardless of the column's type — declare a `FilterDef`
  with an explicit `type` for anything else.
- **A declared field is not inferred either.** A `FieldDef` without `type`
  renders as `"text"`, or `"reference"` when it sets `reference`. `enum`,
  `array` and `reference` columns therefore need an explicit `FieldDef.type`
  (plus `options` / `reference`) to get a richer control.

`enumValues` and `references` are reported for your own use — nothing in the
framework turns them into controls on their own.

### What an implementation must honor

The interface is small, but three of its obligations are load-bearing. Get them
wrong and the admin is still functional — just unsafe.

**Tenant scope.** When `ctx.scopeRequired` is true, every method must constrain
its query with `ctx.applyScope`. `create` included: writing a row outside the
caller's scope is as much a leak as reading one.

**The search allowlist.** `list` may only search columns in `ctx.searchFields`.
Searching every text column turns the search box into a way to confirm values in
columns the operator was never shown.

**Soft delete.** When `ctx.softDelete` is set, `list` and `get` must exclude
stamped rows unless `ctx.includeDeleted` is set, and `delete` must stamp the
column rather than remove the row.

### Declared columns are the boundary

FlowPanel projects every row through the resource's declared surface before it
crosses to the client. An adapter that returns extra columns is not a leak by
itself — but the projection is what makes that safe, so do not bypass it in
custom routes of your own.

### Adapter options

Each shipped adapter takes its own options shape.

`DrizzleAdapterOptions`

| Property | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `db` | `DB` |  |
| `schema` | `Record<string, unknown>` |  |
| `dialect?` | `DrizzleDialect` | Inferred from `schema` when omitted. |
| `parseDates?` | `boolean` | Read zoneless `YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss` strings in a `ctx.sql` result as UTC `Date`s. Turn it off when a text column of your own holds timestamp-shaped strings that `select *` cannot cast. Default: `true`. |

`PrismaAdapterOptions`

| Property | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `prisma` | `P` |  |
| `provider` | `PrismaProvider` | The `datasource` provider from schema.prisma; migrations are dialect-specific. |
| `dmmf?` | `PrismaDmmf` |  |
| `parseDates?` | `boolean` | Read zoneless `YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss` strings in a `ctx.sql` result as UTC `Date`s. Turn it off when a text column of your own holds timestamp-shaped strings that `select *` cannot cast. Default: `true`. |

`BullMQAdapterOptions`

| Property | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `queues` | `Record<string, Queue>` |  |

`bullmqAdapter` is the exception: it takes the queue map itself, not an
options object — `bullmqAdapter({ email: emailQueue, scrape: scrapeQueue })`.
`BullMQAdapterOptions` is exported for symmetry and nothing consumes it.

### Also exported

Each adapter package exposes the pieces its own `Adapter` is assembled from, so
you can reuse one without adopting the whole adapter — a script that only needs
column metadata, or a custom adapter that wants Drizzle's schema inference.

| Package | Also exports |
| --- | --- |
| `@flowpanel/kit/drizzle` | `introspect`, `inferSchema`, `toCsv`, `toJson` |
| `@flowpanel/kit/prisma` | `introspect`, `inferSchema`, `PrismaDmmf` (type) |
| `@flowpanel/kit/bullmq` | `BullMQAdapter` (type) |

`introspect(ref)` returns the same `ResourceIntrospection` the framework reads;
`inferSchema(ref)` returns the `{ create, update, select }` Zod trio a resource
falls back to when it declares no `schema`. `PrismaDmmf` is the shape
`prismaAdapter`'s optional `dmmf` option accepts.

### Export helpers

`@flowpanel/kit/drizzle` also exports `toCsv` and `toJson` — standalone
row serializers, not wired into any route by default.

Both project each row down to `fields` before serializing, the same
declared-columns discipline as the rest of the framework. `toCsv` quotes
values containing a comma, quote, or newline and stringifies `Date`s to ISO
and objects to JSON; `toJson` returns a JSON string of the projected rows.
Use them from a custom export route when `DataTable`'s built-in `exportable`
option — which downloads only the rows currently on screen — isn't enough.

## Scope & realtime

Tenant scoping, the publisher contract, and the rate limiter.

Docs: https://flowpanel.tech/docs/reference/scope-realtime

Documented types: ScopeContext, assertResourceScope, ScopeCheckInput, Publisher, createPublisher, PublisherClient, RedisLike, encodeEnvelope, decodeEnvelope, RateLimiter

Three small contracts that sit under the rest of the framework: how a request is
narrowed to a tenant, how realtime messages travel between instances, and how
throttling counts.

### Scope

A scope is resolved once per request and applied by the adapter to every query.

```ts excerpt
type Scope = Record<string, unknown> | null;
type Session = Record<string, unknown>;
```

`AdminConfig.scope` receives:

`ScopeContext`

| Property | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `req` | `Request` |  |
| `session` | `Session \| null` |  |

```ts excerpt
defineAdmin({
  scope: async ({ session }) => ({ orgId: session?.user?.orgId }),
  // …
});
```

The returned object reaches every context as `ctx.scope`, and the adapter turns
it into a predicate on `ctx.applyScope`.

#### The opt-out is mandatory

Once an admin declares a global `scope`, every resource must say what it does
with it — use it, or opt out with `scope: "bypass"`. A resource that says
nothing throws `FlowpanelAccessError` when it is first queried, rather than
serving another tenant's rows. That is a per-request failure, not a startup
one: `defineAdmin` is pure and runs no such check.

`ScopeCheckInput`

| Property | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hasGlobal` | `boolean` |  |
| `resourceScope` | `"bypass" \| ((...args: unknown[]) => unknown) \| undefined` |  |

That check runs for you inside the request prologue. You only call it directly
when writing an adapter or a route of your own.

See [Multi-tenant scope](/docs/guides/multi-tenant-scope) for the full setup.

### Publisher

The realtime transport. `createPublisher` builds one from `AdminConfig.realtime`;
implement the interface yourself to sit on a bus FlowPanel does not ship.

`Publisher`

| Property | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `publish` | `(channel: string, payload?: unknown) => Promise<void>` |  |
| `subscribe` | `(channel: string, handler: (payload: unknown) => void) => () => void` |  |
| `close?` | `() => Promise<void>` | Release the transport's connections. Publishing afterwards throws. |

```ts excerpt
type PublisherOptions =
  | { driver: "memory" }
  | { driver: "redis"; url?: string; client?: RedisLike; keyPrefix?: string };
```

The memory driver only reaches the process that published, so a second instance
never sees the message. That is fine locally and wrong in production — use the
Redis driver whenever more than one instance serves the admin. The Redis
driver loads `ioredis` on first use and throws if it is not installed; it is an
optional peer dependency.

The redis driver needs one of `url` or `client`, and says which is missing if it
gets neither. `client` takes an `ioredis`-compatible instance you already
configured — TLS, a sentinel, a retry strategy — and FlowPanel then opens no
connection of its own for publishing; it calls `duplicate()` only when something
subscribes, because a subscribed Redis connection can run no other command.
Whichever you pass, nothing connects until the first publish or subscribe:
`defineAdmin` stays pure.

Every connection gets an `error` listener, because an unhandled `error` on a
Redis connection is what takes a Node process down. It logs one line per error
kind rather than one per reconnect attempt, and never rethrows.

`keyPrefix` namespaces channels when several admins share a Redis, and it
defaults to `"flowpanel"` — the wire channel for `resource.orders` is
`flowpanel:resource.orders` unless you set it. It never changes the logical
channel name application code sees. The rate limiter has its own, unrelated
default prefix: `"fp:rl:"`.

Routing is by channel: one channel carries one payload shape, so use a distinct
channel per event kind rather than multiplexing shapes onto one. On the Redis hop
the message body is the payload as JSON — an empty string when there is no
payload — and the channel is the Redis channel name; the `{ channel, payload }`
envelope is added by `stream()` on the way to the browser, and only there. A
payload is serialized in every driver, so the memory driver delivers what Redis
would: a `Date` arrives as an ISO string in development too, and a payload that
cannot be JSON-encoded is rejected with the channel and the reason named,
whether or not this process has a subscriber.

`close()` releases the connections a publisher opened; a `client` you passed in
stays yours, and the `error` listener FlowPanel added to it is removed. A closed
publisher stays closed: `subscribe` opens no connection and hands back a no-op
disposer, and `publish` throws rather than returning quietly.

#### Publishing from a worker

A process that only publishes — a worker, a cron job, a script — imports
`@flowpanel/kit/publish` and nothing else. It needs no admin config, no adapter
and no Next.js, and it opens exactly one connection.

`PublisherClient`

| Property | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `publish` | `(channel: string, payload?: unknown) => Promise<void>` |  |
| `channelFor` | `(resource: string) => string` | The channel a resource's own events travel on: `resource.<name>`. |
| `close` | `() => Promise<void>` | Release the connections this client opened. Idempotent; a host's client is left open. |

`RedisLike`

| Property | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `publish` | `(channel: string, message: string) => Promise<number>` |  |
| `on` | `(event: "error", cb: (err: unknown) => void) => unknown` |  |
| `off?` | `(event: "error", cb: (err: unknown) => void) => unknown` |  |
| `removeListener?` | `(event: "error", cb: (err: unknown) => void) => unknown` |  |
| `duplicate?` | `() => RedisLike & RedisSubscriber` |  |

```ts excerpt
import { createPublisher } from "@flowpanel/kit/publish";

const events = createPublisher({ redis: process.env.REDIS_URL! });
await events.publish(events.channelFor("orders"), { action: "update", id });
```

The SSE envelope is exported next to it, for a consumer that reads the stream
without going through FlowPanel's own client:

`decodeEnvelope` returns `null` for a frame that is not a channelled envelope,
which is how the browser bus drops a foreign frame instead of handing a
subscriber something it cannot read.

See [Realtime with Redis](/docs/guides/realtime-with-redis#publish-from-an-external-worker).

#### The memory driver in a Redis deployment

The publisher is bound per process from `config.realtime`, and rebinds when those
options change, including a `client` that is a different instance than the bound
one — an HMR edit to `realtime` takes effect without restarting the dev server,
while the same config arriving as a different object from another route bundle
does not disturb subscribers that are already connected.

Binding also warns, once per process, when the driver resolves to `memory` while
`REDIS_URL` or `FLOWPANEL_REDIS_URL` is set in the environment:

```
[flowpanel] realtime driver is memory while REDIS_URL is set — other instances
and workers will not receive events; set realtime: { driver: 'redis', url:
process.env.REDIS_URL } in defineAdmin
```

That is the one misconfiguration that looks entirely healthy: every publish
succeeds, the tab that made the change refreshes, and no other instance or tab
ever hears about it.

See [Realtime in production](/docs/guides/realtime).

### RateLimiter

`RateLimiter`

| Property | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `check` | `(key: string) => Promise<boolean>` | Returns true if the request is allowed; false if the limit is exceeded. |

```ts excerpt
function createRateLimiter(opts: RateLimitOptions): RateLimiter;
```

`check` returns `false` when the caller is over the limit, and the request
prologue turns that into a `429`. The key is derived from
`AuthConfig.userId` for `per: "user"`, falling back to the IP when the session
carries no id.

Like the publisher, the memory driver counts per process — a limit of 100 across
four instances is really 400 until you move to Redis.

## Errors

The error hierarchy, its status codes, and what reaches the operator.

Docs: https://flowpanel.tech/docs/reference/errors

Documented types: FlowpanelError, FlowpanelValidationError

Throw one of these from an action, an adapter, or a custom route and FlowPanel
turns it into the right HTTP status with a message that is safe to show. Throw
anything else and the caller gets a generic `500` — the detail is logged, never
sent.

That split is the point of the hierarchy: `safeMessage` is the part you have
decided an operator may read.

### FlowpanelError

The base class. Every other error extends it.

| Property | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `code` | Stable machine-readable tag, e.g. `"validation_failed"`. |
| `safeMessage` | Shown to the operator verbatim. Keep internals out of it. |
| `status` | HTTP status from `FLOWPANEL_ERROR_STATUS[code]`. |

Construct it directly for a case the subclasses do not cover:

```ts excerpt
throw new FlowpanelError("conflict", "This order is already being processed");
```

### The subclasses

| Class | `code` | Status | Default message | Raised by FlowPanel? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `FlowpanelValidationError` | `validation_failed` | 422 | Validation failed | yes |
| `FlowpanelAuthError` | `unauthenticated` | 401 | Authentication required | yours to throw |
| `FlowpanelAccessError` | `forbidden` | 403 | Forbidden | yes |
| `FlowpanelFieldAccessError` | `field_forbidden` | 403 | `Field "x" cannot be changed.` | yes |
| `FlowpanelOperationDisabledError` | `operation_disabled` | 403 | This operation is disabled. | yes |
| `FlowpanelUnknownFieldError` | `unknown_field` | 400 | `Unknown field: "x".` | yes |
| `FlowpanelNotFoundError` | `not_found` | 404 | Not found | yes |
| `FlowpanelConflictError` | `conflict` | 409 | Conflict | no — yours to throw |
| `FlowpanelRateLimitError` | `rate_limited` | 429 | Rate limit exceeded | yes |

Each takes an optional message overriding the default.

The last column matters when you write a `hooks.onError` or a log filter.
FlowPanel raises `FlowpanelAccessError` for rejected admin/resource access and
an unbound tenant scope, `FlowpanelFieldAccessError` for prohibited field
reads/writes, `FlowpanelOperationDisabledError` for disabled mutations,
`FlowpanelUnknownFieldError` for fields outside the resource contract,
`FlowpanelRateLimitError` from the request prologue, and the not-found and
validation errors from resource routes. `FlowpanelAuthError` and
`FlowpanelConflictError` are available for application code. (The render path
still catches `FlowpanelAuthError` if you throw one from a page — see below.)

#### FlowpanelValidationError

The one subclass with extra state: `fieldErrors`, keyed by field name — and it
is the **first** constructor argument, with the message second:

```ts excerpt
constructor(fieldErrors: Record<string, string>, message = "Validation failed");
```

Forms render the entries against the matching inputs instead of showing one
banner.

```ts excerpt
import { FlowpanelValidationError } from "@flowpanel/kit";

throw new FlowpanelValidationError({
  email: "That address is already registered",
});

// with a banner message as well:
throw new FlowpanelValidationError({ email: "Already registered" }, "Could not save");
```

### Config-time errors are not in this hierarchy

`defineAdmin` throws plain `Error`s, deliberately: they happen while your
config module evaluates, long before there is a request to map a status onto.
They carry no `code`, no `safeMessage` and no `status`, and no `hooks.onError`
sees them — the process fails to boot instead.

What they cover: duplicate resource names, dashboard paths and queue keys;
duplicate action keys within one list; a resource or queue named after a
reserved route segment (`dashboards`, `drawer`, `queues`); a column a resource
points at that the adapter does not report; an omitted `columns` on a ref the
adapter cannot introspect; an unresolvable cross-resource reference; and a
`rowClick: "drawer"` with no drawer.

Each names the config path at fault and, where it can, the near match. See
[Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting#defineadmin-throws-when-the-app-boots)
for the full table.

#### Did you mean

A name that is not registered but is close to one that is gets the suggestion
appended to the error: an exact match once casing and `_`/`-` are ignored, else
the closest name within an edit distance of two.

```text
resource "users" points at column "emial" via columns[0], but the adapter
reports no such column. Did you mean "email"? Known columns: "id", "email".
```

It applies to `columns`, `filters`, `expose`, `defaultSort.field`, `rowKey`,
`create.fields` / `update.fields` names, and to the resource a
`detail.tabs[]` / `drawer.tabs[]` entry or a `reference` points at.

#### Warnings that do not stop the boot

Some config problems are real but do not justify refusing to start. `defineAdmin`
collects them on the resolved config as `warnings: readonly string[]`, prints each
one once per process in development, and `flowpanel doctor` lists them. (`doctor`
evaluates `flowpanel.config.ts` to read them; if that fails — a missing
`DATABASE_URL`, say — it prints one line saying the warnings were not checked
instead of passing silently.)

The one warning today is a create form that cannot succeed:

```text
resource users: create is enabled but required column `email` has no field;
creation will always fail
```

It fires for a column the adapter reports as non-nullable, not generated, not
defaulted (`ColumnMeta.hasDefault`, which both shipped adapters populate) and not
the primary key, when nothing a create write carries would fill it: not
`create.fields`, not `columns` when `create.fields` is absent, and not
`create.defaultValues`. An adapter that does not report `hasDefault` makes a
defaulted column look required; declare it in `create.fields` or
`create.defaultValues` to say otherwise.

### On the page render path

`FlowpanelAuthError` and `FlowpanelAccessError` thrown while rendering a page are
caught by the shell, not surfaced as a crash:

- `auth.signInUrl` is set → redirect there.
- `auth.forbiddenUrl` is set and the visitor is signed in → redirect there.
- Neither → an inline "Sign in required" or "Access denied" panel.

Other errors propagate to your Next.js error boundary — except for a failed
adapter read, which has a surface of its own.

#### A query that failed

When the adapter's `list` or `get` throws while a list page, a detail page or a
related tab renders, FlowPanel renders its own card in place of the data instead
of letting the page crash into the host's error boundary. The card names the
resource and the operation through `labels.errors.queryTitle`, adds
`labels.errors.queryHint`, and carries the request id the failure was logged
under:

```text
users: list failed
Check the column list and the database schema. Details are in the server log.
Request 5f3c…
```

The cause always goes to `console.error` with that same id, and outside
production the card shows the message too. Nothing else about it changes with the
environment. A `FlowpanelError` — an access denial, a not-found — keeps
travelling, so the auth boundary above still sees it, and so does a `redirect()`
thrown from your own code.

Dashboard and detail-tab widgets already have their own boundary: a widget whose
query or render throws becomes one failed card, with its copy from
`labels.errors.widgetTitle`, `widgetHint` and `retry`.

### Returning versus throwing

Inside an action's `run` you have both options:

```ts excerpt
run: async (row, input, ctx) => {
  if (row.status === "refunded") {
    return { ok: false, error: "Already refunded" };   // 200 with a failure body
  }
  throw new FlowpanelConflictError("Order is locked"); // 409
}
```

Return `{ ok: false }` for an outcome the operator caused and can fix — the UI
shows the message next to the action. Throw when the request itself was not
valid, and you want the status code to say so.

### Errors the routes produce themselves

Some generated-UI responses never pass through the hierarchy at all — the
route answers directly with a string `error`. These compatibility routes are
distinct from the v1 JSON CRUD API and protected controllers, whose
`FlowpanelResultError` contains `code`, `message`, optional `fieldErrors`, and
`requestId`.

#### 400 — malformed request body

A POST that declares `Content-Type: application/json` but carries a body that
does not parse is rejected before anything else runs:

```json
{ "ok": false, "error": "invalid JSON body" }
```

That covers the row-, bulk-, dashboard- and drawer-action routes and the
inline-cell update. A non-JSON content type is parsed as form data instead and
never reaches this branch.

#### 404 — unknown resource, action or dashboard

The message depends on `NODE_ENV`, on purpose. In **production** it is terse,
so the response confirms nothing about what does exist:

```json
{ "ok": false, "error": "resource not found" }
```

Outside production it names what was requested and what is registered, which
turns "why is my action 404-ing" into a one-look answer:

```json
{
  "ok": false,
  "error": "action not found: \"refnud\". Registered actions: \"refund\", \"cancel\"."
}
```

`kind` is one of `resource`, `action` or `dashboard`.

#### 403 / 422 from the guard pipeline

`403 Cross-origin write requests are not allowed.` when the default browser
origin guard blocks a mutation; `403 This admin is read-only.` when
`readOnly: true` blocks a write;
`422 too many ids (max 1000)` when a bulk action exceeds its cap;
`422 validation failed` with an `issues` array when an action `form` fails
validation. See [Actions → Validation](/docs/reference/actions#validation).

## CLI

The flowpanel command-line interface.

Docs: https://flowpanel.tech/docs/reference/cli

FlowPanel ships a small CLI in the `@flowpanel/cli` package. Bootstrap a
project with `pnpm dlx @flowpanel/cli init` — no install needed up front.
`init` adds `@flowpanel/cli` as a devDependency, so every later command
runs as `pnpm flowpanel <command>`. The shipped subcommands are `init`,
`migrate`, `doctor`, `eject`, `dev`, and `new`.

The CLI detects your package manager from the lockfile and uses it
throughout — `init` installs with it, `dev` launches Next.js through its
runner, and every "run this next" hint is printed in its syntax. The samples
below use pnpm; substitute your own.

`flowpanel [options] [command]` — Admin panels the fast way
- `-V, --version` output the version number

`flowpanel init [options]` — Initialize FlowPanel in this project
- `--yes` Accept detected defaults without prompting (CI mode)
- `--dry-run` Print the filesystem plan without writing or installing
- `--json` Emit machine-readable JSON (implies --yes)
- `--path <url>` Mount the admin at a static URL, for example /ops/admin
- `--db <module>` Local module exporting your db or prisma client
- `--schema <module>` Local module exporting your Drizzle schema
- `--auth <module>` Local module exporting getSession(request)
- `--dev-auth` Explicitly use an open development-only admin identity

`flowpanel migrate [options]` — Apply SQL migrations from flowpanel/migrations/
- `--dry-run` Print migrations that would be applied without running them
- `--json` Emit machine-readable JSON

`flowpanel doctor [options]` — Check FlowPanel health and wiring
- `--fix` Auto-fix missing route files from templates
- `--dry-run` Show fixes without writing (use with --fix)
- `--json` Emit machine-readable JSON
- `--path <url>` Resolved admin URL when the config uses a dynamic path

`flowpanel eject [options] <target> [name]` — Eject a FlowPanel piece into your app/admin folder. Targets: resource <name>, dashboard <path>, layout.
- `<target>`
- `[name]`
- `--force` Overwrite files if they already exist
- `--dry-run` Print the filesystem plan without writing
- `--json` Emit machine-readable JSON

`flowpanel dev [options]` — Run Next.js dev server (and bull-board if REDIS_URL is set)
- `--port <port>` Next.js dev port Default: `3000`.
- `--no-board` Skip the bull-board server even if REDIS_URL is set

`flowpanel new [options] <resource>` — Add a resource(...) entry to flowpanel.config.ts
- `<resource>`
- `--table <expr>` First argument expression (default: schema.<resource>)
- `--kind <kind>` Adapter kind: drizzle (default) or prisma Default: `drizzle`.
- `--dry-run` Print the filesystem plan without writing
- `--json` Emit machine-readable JSON

Every command supports `--help`; the root command supports `--version`.
Success exits `0`, validation or execution failures exit non-zero, and fatal
errors show a concise message. Set `FLOWPANEL_DEBUG=1` when you also need the
underlying stack trace.

Mutating commands build a complete filesystem plan before the first write.
`--dry-run` prints that plan; `--json` emits a machine-readable result for CI.
Writes use atomic replacement and a rollback journal, so a later failure
restores earlier files instead of leaving a half-written scaffold. Existing
files with different content are reported as conflicts, not overwritten.

### flowpanel init

`flowpanel init [options]` — Initialize FlowPanel in this project
- `--yes` Accept detected defaults without prompting (CI mode)
- `--dry-run` Print the filesystem plan without writing or installing
- `--json` Emit machine-readable JSON (implies --yes)
- `--path <url>` Mount the admin at a static URL, for example /ops/admin
- `--db <module>` Local module exporting your db or prisma client
- `--schema <module>` Local module exporting your Drizzle schema
- `--auth <module>` Local module exporting getSession(request)
- `--dev-auth` Explicitly use an open development-only admin identity

Detect your stack (Next.js, Drizzle/Prisma, auth helper), pick the
matching config template, install `@flowpanel/kit` + `@flowpanel/cli`,
and scaffold the wiring files. Both Drizzle and Prisma are supported in a
single command; the CLI picks based on your installed dependencies
(Drizzle wins if both are present).

The stylesheet lands at `styles/admin.css`, or at `src/styles/admin.css` when
the project keeps its source under `src/` — the CLI matches your layout rather
than always writing to the repo root.

```text
◇  Detected stack ─────────────────────────────────────╮
│  Next.js 16.3.1 · TypeScript · Drizzle · Tailwind 4  │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
◇  7 written
◇  Wrote ─────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│  flowpanel.config.ts                                    │
│  app/admin/[[...slug]]/page.tsx                         │
│  app/api/flowpanel/[...route]/route.ts                  │
│  app/api/flowpanel/stream/route.ts                      │
│  styles/admin.css                                       │
│  flowpanel/migrations/0001_init.sql                     │
│  app/admin/layout.tsx (imports the admin stylesheet)    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
◇  Installed @flowpanel/kit, @flowpanel/cli
```

What varies:

- **`src/`** — every `app/` path becomes `src/app/`, and `styles/admin.css`
  becomes `src/styles/admin.css`, when the project uses a `src/` layout.
- **Admin mount** — `/admin` by default, `/flowpanel` when `/admin` is occupied,
  or an explicit `--path /ops/admin`. Route groups are included in collision checks;
  a busy fallback stops installation before any writes.
- **Admin layout** — imports the stylesheet under the chosen route. The existing
  root layout is never patched. Without a shared root layout, the admin segment
  receives its own root layout. That layout reads the `x-nonce` request header and
  forwards it to `ThemeScript`, so the pre-hydration theme script survives a strict
  `script-src` policy — but only when your own middleware sets `x-nonce` on the
  request and emits the matching `script-src 'nonce-…'` header. FlowPanel does not
  write that middleware, and with no `x-nonce` present the header read returns
  `null` and the script is rendered without a nonce, exactly as before. Reading
  `headers()` makes the admin segment dynamically rendered; it already was, because
  `auth.session` reads the request. Existing host theme/CSP integration is left to
  the application; `ThemeScript` accepts its nonce.
- **Authentication** — `init` reads `package.json` for `better-auth`, `next-auth`,
  `@clerk/nextjs` or `lucia` and names what it recognised in the detected-stack
  note and the outro. When the auth module it found exports that provider's own
  instance rather than a `getSession`, it writes
  `server/lib/flowpanel-session.ts` built on the matching preset
  ([`withBetterAuth`](/docs/guides/auth-with-better-auth),
  [`withClerk`](/docs/guides/auth-with-clerk), `withNextAuth`, `withLucia`) and
  points the config at it. A module that already exports `getSession` is left
  alone, and an unrecognised project still gets the closed `getSession` adapter.
  Connect your role mapping either way; async role lookups are supported. Use
  `--dev-auth` only to explicitly opt into an open development-only identity.
- **Stylesheet** — `admin.css` imports `@flowpanel/kit/styles/admin.css`, the
  precompiled and isolated FlowPanel stylesheet. It does not require Tailwind,
  a Tailwind config, source/content directives, or a PostCSS plugin.
- **The install step** uses the package manager it detected — npm, pnpm, yarn
  or bun — and is skipped for packages already in your `package.json`.
- **The next-steps outro** is written in that manager's own vocabulary
  (`pnpm exec flowpanel migrate` vs `npx flowpanel migrate`, and so on).

#### When `init` stops

- **No Next.js in `package.json`** — aborts, exit `1`, with the install
  command for your package manager.
- **No Drizzle and no Prisma** — aborts, exit `1`, same treatment.
- **No TTY and no `--yes`, `--dry-run` or `--json`** — `init` asks questions, so a non-interactive run
  without `--yes` exits `1` immediately: *"init asks questions and this run
  has no interactive terminal. Re-run with --yes to accept the detected
  defaults."* Pass `--yes` in CI.
- **A failed dependency install** does not roll back the files. It prints the
  package manager's own last lines, the commands to run by hand, and sets
  exit code `1` so the run is not mistaken for a success.
- **A dependency that installs but cannot be used** is treated the same way. A
  `@flowpanel/kit` from another minor, or a project-local `@flowpanel/cli` from
  another minor than the one you ran, is listed in `dependencies.failed` with
  its own recovery command and exits `1`. A different patch or a matching
  preview of the same minor is accepted.

Re-running `init` is idempotent: matching generated files become `skip`.
If any target exists with different content, the plan reports a conflict and
nothing is written. Merge that file manually, then rerun. `--yes` accepts
detected paths; it does not grant permission to overwrite source.

### flowpanel migrate

`flowpanel migrate [options]` — Apply SQL migrations from flowpanel/migrations/
- `--dry-run` Print migrations that would be applied without running them
- `--json` Emit machine-readable JSON

Apply SQL migrations from `flowpanel/migrations/`. The CLI dynamically
imports your `flowpanel.config.ts` (via `jiti`) so it can reach the
adapter's `db` instance and run the migration there.

```bash
$ pnpm flowpanel migrate
```

Use `--dry-run` to inspect migration files without importing your config or
opening a database connection. Because it deliberately cannot know the applied
state, it lists every SQL file and reports `appliedStateKnown: false` in JSON.
Run the command without `--dry-run` to compare those files with the database.
Add `--json` for a stable pending/applied payload. The CLI tracks applied IDs in
`_flowpanel_migrations`.

Each pending file is handed to the selected migration executor. A modern
adapter provides one `applyMigration(id, sql)` operation; the compatibility
executor composes the legacy `runMigrationSql` and `markMigrationApplied`
hooks. On PostgreSQL and SQLite the modern operation keeps SQL and bookkeeping
in one transaction. MySQL DDL implicitly commits, so review and back up
production migrations.

The applied-ID list is a preflight snapshot, not a process lock. Both shipped
adapters serialize at the database, recheck the ID under that lock and treat a
concurrent duplicate as a no-op. PostgreSQL and SQLite keep the file and its
marker in one transaction. MySQL implicitly commits DDL, so it is serialized
instead: Drizzle pins a connection behind an advisory lock, Prisma claims a
durable row that also records where a failed run stopped.

Custom adapters should implement `applyMigration` and `listAppliedMigrations`.
During the 0.2 upgrade, the CLI still accepts the legacy `runMigrationSql` plus
`markMigrationApplied` pair and warns that it is non-atomic and does not
serialize concurrent migrators; JSON output then exposes
`migrationMode: "legacy-hooks"` and a non-empty `warnings` array, so CI can
reject it explicitly. Both shipped adapters implement the locked operation and
never take that path.

Both adapters reject dialect-specific procedural scripts without PostgreSQL
dollar-quoted bodies before executing them; Prisma also rejects MySQL
executable comments and client directives such as `DELIMITER`. Use the ORM's
native migration workflow for those files.

Every command reads `.env.local` and then `.env` from the working directory
before it runs, the same order Next.js uses, so a `DATABASE_URL` that already
works for `next dev` works here too. Variables already set in the shell win, so
`DATABASE_URL=… pnpm flowpanel migrate` still overrides the file. When the
connection fails and no `DATABASE_URL` is set anywhere, the CLI says so instead
of printing a driver stack trace; `FLOWPANEL_DEBUG=1` brings the stack back.

`jiti` is loaded on demand; when it is missing the command prints the install
line for **your** package manager (`pnpm add -D jiti`, `npm install --save-dev
jiti`, …) and exits `1`.

### flowpanel doctor

`flowpanel doctor [options]` — Check FlowPanel health and wiring
- `--fix` Auto-fix missing route files from templates
- `--dry-run` Show fixes without writing (use with --fix)
- `--json` Emit machine-readable JSON
- `--path <url>` Resolved admin URL when the config uses a dynamic path

Run the wiring checks, in this order:

- Next.js ≥ 16.3 and < 17, and TypeScript installed
- an ORM the adapters support — Drizzle or Prisma
- `flowpanel.config.ts` exists
- the four generated files exist: the API route, the SSE route, the seed
  migration, and the catch-all admin page
- only one reachable `@flowpanel/core` installation across the installed
  dependency graph, including package-local peers and third-party plugins.
  Stale pnpm store entries are ignored; uninstalled projects skip this check
- no destructive row/bulk action declared without a `confirm`
- `tsc --noEmit` passes

Mount checks follow URL segments through route groups, parallel slots, and
intercepting routes. Existing pages inside the selected admin branch remain
protected. Sibling dynamic routes such as `[locale]` and parent catch-all fallbacks
can coexist with a static admin branch; Next gives the static branch precedence.
The selected admin URL is therefore reserved for FlowPanel even if a fallback
previously matched it.

```bash
$ pnpm flowpanel doctor
$ pnpm flowpanel doctor --fix
$ pnpm flowpanel doctor --fix --dry-run
```

`--fix` creates whichever of the four generated files are missing from the
same templates `init` uses. The fix is one transaction; `--dry-run` shows it
without writing. The other failures have no auto-fix and print a hint instead.

Exit code is non-zero when any check fails — wire it into CI to catch
drift on every PR.

### flowpanel eject

`flowpanel eject [options] <target> [name]` — Eject a FlowPanel piece into your app/admin folder. Targets: resource <name>, dashboard <path>, layout.
- `<target>`
- `[name]`
- `--force` Overwrite files if they already exist
- `--dry-run` Print the filesystem plan without writing
- `--json` Emit machine-readable JSON

Eject one of three targets — `resource`, `dashboard`, or `layout` —
into your repo. See [Customization / Eject](/docs/customization/eject).

```bash
$ pnpm flowpanel eject resource users
$ pnpm flowpanel eject dashboard "/monitoring"
$ pnpm flowpanel eject layout
```

It lists every file it wrote, then comments the matching config entry out
(uncomment to revert). Template files and the config edit are committed as one
rollback-safe transaction. Pass `--force` to explicitly replace an existing
eject target; without it, a conflict aborts before any file changes.

### flowpanel dev

`flowpanel dev [options]` — Run Next.js dev server (and bull-board if REDIS_URL is set)
- `--port <port>` Next.js dev port Default: `3000`.
- `--no-board` Skip the bull-board server even if REDIS_URL is set

Wrapper around `next dev` that also spawns `bull-board` when a
`scripts/board-server.mts` (or `.ts`) file is present and `REDIS_URL` is set.

```bash
$ pnpm flowpanel dev --port 3000
```

Both children are launched through the **detected** package manager's runner —
`pnpm exec next dev`, `npx next dev`, `yarn next dev`, `bunx next dev` — so
the local binaries resolve whichever manager installed them. Output is
prefixed `[next]` / `[board]`, and either child exiting shuts the other down.

Pass `--no-board` to skip the queue dashboard even when Redis is up. With
`REDIS_URL` set but no `scripts/board-server.mts` or `.ts` on disk, the board is skipped
with a one-line note rather than an error.

### flowpanel new

`flowpanel new [options] <resource>` — Add a resource(...) entry to flowpanel.config.ts
- `<resource>`
- `--table <expr>` First argument expression (default: schema.<resource>)
- `--kind <kind>` Adapter kind: drizzle (default) or prisma Default: `drizzle`.
- `--dry-run` Print the filesystem plan without writing
- `--json` Emit machine-readable JSON

Append a `resource(...)` entry to your existing
`flowpanel.config.ts` without re-running `init`.

```bash
$ pnpm flowpanel new posts
```

```text
└  Added resource "posts" to flowpanel.config.ts
```

It writes `resource(schema.posts, { columns: ["id"] })` into the `resources`
array — creating the array when `defineAdmin` has none — and **adds `resource`
to the existing `@flowpanel/kit` import** when the config does not already
bind that name, so the file compiles as written. Existing comments in the
array are preserved (the entry is spliced as text, not reprinted).

Before writing, a Drizzle-kind run resolves the config's `import * as schema`
line and checks that the module really exports `posts`. A miss aborts with
exit `1` and lists what the schema does export; an unverifiable case (no
`import * as schema`, an unresolvable specifier) warns and writes anyway.
A resource that already exists aborts with exit `1`.

Flags: `--table <expr>` overrides the first argument (default
`schema.<resource>`, and skips the schema check); `--kind drizzle|prisma`
toggles the template (default `drizzle`; `prisma` writes
`resource<unknown>("posts", …)`).

`--dry-run` shows the config modification without applying it. `--json`
returns the same plan/result envelope used by `init`, `doctor` and `eject`.

## Smoke testing

Walk every page of a generated admin in one Playwright call and fail on errors, broken links and accessibility violations.

Docs: https://flowpanel.tech/docs/reference/testing

Documented types: smokeAdmin, SmokeAdminOptions, SmokeAdminReport, A11yViolation

`@flowpanel/test` is a dev-time package: one function that walks a running
admin the way an operator does and fails the build when a page is broken. It
is not part of `@flowpanel/kit` and never reaches your application bundle.

```sh
pnpm add -D @flowpanel/test @playwright/test
```

`@playwright/test` is a required peer. `@axe-core/playwright` is an optional
one — install it to turn the accessibility assertions on.

### smokeAdmin

```ts excerpt
import { test } from "@playwright/test";
import { smokeAdmin } from "@flowpanel/test";

test("the admin is healthy", async ({ page }) => {
  await smokeAdmin(page, { basePath: "/admin", a11y: true });
});
```

The walk starts at `basePath`, reads the navigation — `[data-flowpanel-nav]`,
which both shell modes render, and opens every
dashboard and resource list it links to. On each list it activates the first
row and follows wherever that resource sends it — the row's own detail page
when `rowClick: "detail"`, the URL-synced drawer when `rowClick: "drawer"`. A
row the projection cannot identify is inert, and the walk leaves it alone
rather than failing.

### What it asserts

| Assertion | How it fails |
| --- | --- |
| Every navigation answers below 400 | `<route>: responded 500` |
| Nothing wrote to `console.error` | `console.error: <text>` |
| No page rendered `[data-fp-error]` | `<route>: rendered a FlowPanel error surface` |
| Zero WCAG 2.2 AA violations, with `a11y` | `<route>: axe <rule> (<impact>)` |
| The navigation has at least one route | `smokeAdmin found no navigation under <basePath> …` |

`[data-fp-error]` is the attribute FlowPanel's own error surfaces carry: the card
a failed widget leaves behind, the card a failed adapter read renders, a drawer
whose payload read failed, and the error tone of the health banner. Finding one
means the page rendered, so no navigation failed, but a read underneath it did.

A walk that discovers no routes beyond the entry page is a failure, not a pass. A
`basePath` that points at the wrong mount, an unsigned-in session or a shell whose
navigation carries no `data-flowpanel-nav` would otherwise produce a green report
about a page nobody walked.

The walk waits for the `main` landmark to become visible rather than for the
network to go idle: an admin holding a realtime connection never reaches
`networkidle`.

### Options and report

`SmokeAdminOptions`

| Property | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `basePath?` | `string` | Where the admin is mounted, matching `createFlowpanel`'s `basePath`. Default: `"/admin"`. |
| `cookie?` | `{ name: string; value: string; domain?: string }` | Session cookie added before the walk, for an admin behind authentication. |
| `resources?` | `string[]` | Restrict the walk to these nav segments — `"customers"` for `/admin/customers`, `"/"` for the landing page. Every nav entry is visited when this is omitted. |
| `a11y?` | `boolean` | Run axe against every visited route. Needs `@axe-core/playwright`; the walk skips the scan, rather than failing, when it does not resolve. Default: `false`. |
| `maxRows?` | `number` | How many rows of each list the walk opens. Default: `1`. |

`SmokeAdminReport`

| Property | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `visited` | `string[]` | Every route the walk loaded, in order, including rows it opened. |
| `consoleErrors` | `string[]` |  |
| `a11yViolations` | `A11yViolation[]` |  |

`A11yViolation`

| Property | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `route` | `string` |  |
| `id` | `string` |  |
| `impact?` | `string` |  |

`A11yViolation` is the element type of `SmokeAdminReport.a11yViolations`: one axe
rule, and the route it was found on.

`smokeAdmin` resolves with the report when everything passed, and throws an
`Error` whose message lists each problem and then the whole report as JSON, so
a failing run tells you which route broke without a second pass.

```ts excerpt
import { smokeAdmin } from "@flowpanel/test";

const report = await smokeAdmin(page, {
  basePath: "/admin",
  cookie: { name: "session", value: process.env.E2E_SESSION ?? "" },
  resources: ["/", "customers", "orders"],
  maxRows: 3,
  a11y: true,
});

console.log(`${report.visited.length} routes visited`);
```

`resources` takes nav segments, not paths: `"/"` is the landing dashboard and
`"customers"` is `/admin/customers`. `cookie` is added against the admin's own
origin unless you give it an explicit `domain`.

### Authentication

An admin behind a session cookie needs that cookie before the walk can see
anything. Pass it as `cookie`, or sign in with your project's own Playwright
fixture first — `smokeAdmin` reuses whatever context the page already has.

```ts excerpt
import { smokeAdmin } from "@flowpanel/test";

await page.goto("/login");
await page.getByLabel("Email").fill("admin@example.com");
await page.getByLabel("Password").fill(process.env.E2E_PASSWORD ?? "");
await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Sign in" }).click();

await smokeAdmin(page);
```

## ESLint plugin

Five rules that catch config mistakes the type system cannot.

Docs: https://flowpanel.tech/docs/reference/eslint-plugin

`@flowpanel/eslint-plugin` is a separate, optional package. It catches the
mistakes that survive type-checking: a client component importing server code,
a destructive action with no confirm, two resources fighting over one name.

Pre-1.0. The rule *names* are stable; their options and message text may still
change before 1.0.

### Install

```bash
pnpm add -D @flowpanel/eslint-plugin
```

It peers on `eslint >= 8`, and the shipped config is flat-config (ESLint 9)
shaped.

### Setup

```ts excerpt
import flowpanel from "@flowpanel/eslint-plugin";

export default [flowpanel.configs.recommended];
```

`configs.recommended` registers the plugin under the `flowpanel` namespace and
turns on all five rules at the severities in the table below. To pick rules by
hand instead:

```ts excerpt
import flowpanel from "@flowpanel/eslint-plugin";

export default [
  {
    plugins: { flowpanel },
    rules: {
      "flowpanel/prefer-shorthand-filter": "warn",
      "flowpanel/audit-row-action-needs-confirm": "error",
      "flowpanel/no-server-import-in-client": "error",
      "flowpanel/require-unique-resource-names": "error",
      "flowpanel/no-typo-column-keyword": "warn",
    },
  },
];
```

The package's default export is the plugin object; `configs` and `rules` are
also named exports.

### The rules

| Rule | Recommended | Type | Fixable |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`no-server-import-in-client`](#no-server-import-in-client) | `error` | problem | no |
| [`audit-row-action-needs-confirm`](#audit-row-action-needs-confirm) | `error` | problem | no |
| [`require-unique-resource-names`](#require-unique-resource-names) | `error` | problem | no |
| [`prefer-shorthand-filter`](#prefer-shorthand-filter) | `warn` | suggestion | yes |
| [`no-typo-column-keyword`](#no-typo-column-keyword) | `warn` | problem | no |

#### `no-server-import-in-client`

In a file that opens with `"use client"`, importing a server-only module ships
server code — and whatever secrets it closes over — to the browser. The rule
flags:

- `server-only` and any `*/server-only` specifier;
- an app-local path containing a `/server/` segment, or ending in `/server`;
- `@/db` and `@/db/…`, plus the `~/db`, `src/db` and `./db` variants.

Only alias and relative specifiers (`@/`, `~/`, `./`, `../`, `src/`) count as
app-local, so package entry points like `next/server` are left alone.
`import type` is skipped — it is erased before bundling.

#### `audit-row-action-needs-confirm`

An entry in `actions:` or `bulkActions:` with `variant: "destructive"` and no
sibling `confirm:` is reported. You have to write the message, so there is no
autofix.

```ts excerpt
// bad
actions: [{ key: "delete", label: "Delete", variant: "destructive", run }];

// good
actions: [
  {
    key: "delete",
    label: "Delete",
    variant: "destructive",
    confirm: "Are you sure?",
    run,
  },
];
```

#### `require-unique-resource-names`

Within one `defineAdmin({ resources: [...] })` call, every `resource()` entry
must resolve to a unique name — the same rule `defineAdmin` throws on at
runtime, moved to lint time. The name comes from `opts.name` when it is a
string literal, otherwise from a string ref (`resource("User", …)`).

Bare identifiers — the decomposed `resources: [users, orders]` layout — are
resolved through their `const x = resource(…)` declaration when it lives in
the same file; otherwise the identifier itself has to be unique. A name that
can only be known from the ref at runtime is left to the runtime validator.

#### `prefer-shorthand-filter`

When every entry of an `options:` array inside `filters: [...]` has
`label === value`, the array can be a plain string array — the runtime
normalizes both to the same thing. Autofixable.

```ts excerpt
// bad
filters: [
  {
    field: "status",
    type: "select",
    options: [
      { label: "active", value: "active" },
      { label: "archived", value: "archived" },
    ],
  },
];

// good
filters: [{ field: "status", type: "select", options: ["active", "archived"] }];
```

#### `no-typo-column-keyword`

A heuristic check for the camelCase slips that a `Record<string, unknown>` row
type will not catch — see
[when column names are only `string`](/docs/build/resources#typos-and-column-validation).
Today it knows a short list: `userid`, `createdat`, `updatedat`, `isactive`.

Deliberately **not** autofixable: `columns` is not a FlowPanel-exclusive
property name, and a lower-case column can be intentional, so
`eslint --fix` must not rewrite it. Schema-aware validation is tracked
separately; `defineAdmin`'s introspect-time check already covers the
schema-aware half at config time.
